title: How Barbie, the Toy World's Idol, Grew Old
excerpt: Barbie once set the trends in toy buying as a rebel. Now she is being cast aside: she is no longer new.
body:
Barbie once set the trends in toy buying as a rebel. Now she is being cast aside: she is no longer new.

Few people have never heard of Barbie. Fewer may know that Barbie made Mattel the world's biggest toy company, a title it held until Lego took it in the second half of 2014. And Bryan Stockton is probably the first CEO to lose his job over poor Barbie sales.

At the end of January, Mattel reported its results for the fourth quarter of 2014. In the all-important holiday shopping season, global sales fell 6% year on year to US$1.99 billion, and net profit plunged 59% to US$149 million. In the toy business the fourth quarter matters enormously: holidays such as Black Friday and Christmas bring in most of the industry's profit for the year.

Barbie, Mattel's best-selling brand, fell the furthest. In the third quarter of 2014 Barbie sales dropped 21%. Barbie once brought in US$1.8 billion a year, but in the 12 months to September her sales were just US$100 million.

Mattel's rivals Lego and Disney are in a very different position. Lego is growing fast: its global revenue in 2013 was double that of 2009. Disney's *Frozen*, the highest-grossing film in the company's history, has spawned dolls that pushed Barbie aside to become the most popular toys for girls.

After the results came out, Mattel spokesman Alex Clark said: "Mattel spent heavily on marketing for this Christmas shopping season, but the results fell far short of what we expected, and our board feels an urgent need to change leadership." Mattel said the board had named Christopher Sinclair chairman and interim CEO.

But Mattel's problems are not the kind a new CEO can fix quickly.

### 1. In the five years since the financial crisis, Mattel's sales growth has kept falling

From 2010 to 2014, Mattel's year-on-year global sales growth fell from 8% to -7%. For Wall Street investors fixated on growth, this is very bad news, and Bryan Stockton, CEO since late 2011, is widely seen as bearing the blame.

![Chart: Mattel's year-on-year global sales growth, 2010-2014](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142421SMtj2U4o0q6G1HNy.jpg-w600)

Stockton did try to lift sales by expanding overseas; it was one of his main moves after taking over. "The global middle class is expected to grow from 559 million households in 2011 to 766 million in 2020," he once said.

The global push has not worked well. The US home market, always the largest source of revenue, has slipped from 54% of sales to about 50%. Mattel's US sales were US$346 million in 2010 and had barely moved by 2013, at US$383 million. And the emerging markets that were supposed to be promising have not made up for the near-stagnation at home.

![Chart: Mattel's sales by region](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142422Kz0FXImE8TRPM7WY.jpg-w600)

Take China, which foreign brands of every kind have treated as a growth engine. In 2011 Barbie closed her first global flagship store, in Shanghai. Earlier still, in 2007, Mattel was hit by a "poison doll" scandal.

That year the US Consumer Product Safety Commission found that paint on Mattel toys contained excessive lead, which could seriously harm children's brain development. It required Mattel to recall 967,000 plastic toys made by Lida. Lida Toy Ltd. was badly hurt, and its deputy chairman, Zhang Shuhong, hanged himself. Mattel's reputation began to suffer.

![Mattel's 2007 lead-paint toy recall](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142422iftBngRb4Ex6WUhA.jpg-w600)

### 2. Barbie, the best seller, has fallen the furthest

In 1959 Ruth Handler, one of Mattel's founders, designed the 11.5-inch Barbie doll, modeled on the German toy Bild Lilli. The first Barbie wore a zebra-striped swimsuit and a ponytail. Billed as a grown-up fashion model and made in Japan, she sold 35,000 units as soon as she went on sale.

Early Barbie's slogan was "I Can Be… Barbie." Mattel was hinting to children and their mothers that Barbie was a grown-up they could identify with and a good role model to follow, breaking with the old tradition of doll play as caregiving and companionship.

The suggestion worked very well. Barbie became the best-known toy of her day and set a sales record of two dolls sold every second.

Barbie is now 56. Ten years ago she made up 30% of Mattel's annual revenue; today she makes up only 20%.

![Chart: Barbie's share of Mattel's annual revenue](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142423wEtp6jdsHQRKYA4X.jpg-w600)

After the Shanghai flagship closed, Barbie's annual sales began a clear, steady decline from 2012: down 3% in 2012, 6% in 2013 and 16% in 2014. Since 2000, Barbie's US sales alone have plunged 50%.

### 3. Above all, Mattel has stopped innovating

In 1945 Ruth Handler, her husband Elliot Handler and Harold Matson founded Mattel in a garage in Southern California. They started out making picture frames and only later turned to toys.

After more than 60 years of mergers and acquisitions, Mattel now has four subsidiaries: Fisher-Price, Mega Brands, HIT Entertainment and Playground Productions. Its main toy brands include Barbie; Monster High, a fantasy doll line launched in 2010; American Girl, launched in 1986; Matchbox cars; toys based on the American cartoon *He-Man and the Masters of the Universe*; and Hot Wheels model cars.

Mattel holds 16% of the US$20 billion US toy market, almost twice as much as second-place Hasbro. But even this legendary toy company has to face its own aging.

Mattel's results single out four lines: Barbie, the baby and toddler brand Fisher-Price, American Girl dolls and the Hot Wheels model cars. They were launched in 1959, 1930, 1986 and 1968 respectively. Yes, all more than 30 years ago.

![Chart: Mattel's four core brands and their launch years](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142423Do1ljZ9QV6eH7YT8.jpg-w600)

In 2012 Mattel bought HIT Entertainment, owner of *Thomas & Friends*. In 2014 it bought the building-block maker Mega Brands. As far back as the early 1980s it moved into video games in partnership with Nintendo. But through bad timing and strategy, none of these lines took off.

In early 2014, Stockton, then CEO, had to admit that Mattel's product innovation was not as strong as it used to be.

### 4. Barbie's market has changed beyond recognition, but Barbie has barely changed at all

New rivals

According to NPD Group, a global market research firm whose data cover about 80% of the market, the two best-selling US toys of 2014 were *Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles* and *Frozen* merchandise. Mattel's Hot Wheels came third; Barbie fell to eighth. In the US National Retail Federation's survey of the toys girls most wanted for the holidays, a doll based on Elsa, the princess in Disney's *Frozen*, knocked Barbie off the top spot for the first time in 11 years. About 20% of parents planned to buy one for their children.

Barbie, too, has long made money by selling spin-offs: accessories of every kind, and an assortment of "boyfriends" and "friends." Mattel has kept developing her: she now has more than 80 careers, 43 pets and five sisters, and there are regional editions for different parts of the world. Yet on the whole she offers little that catches the eye.

Electronics are also emerging as a new rival to traditional dolls. On the 2014 US toy sales chart, the LeapFrog Explorer Licensed Software Asst game console and Samsung's Galaxy kids' tablet both outsold Barbie. Games that cost just US$1.99 to US$2.99 on Android and iOS are reshaping the whole toy industry.

![Chart: best-selling US toys of 2014](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142424VlyjDKaRIC3UO7qm.jpg-w600)

Marketing that no longer works

You may not know that Mattel was the first toy company to advertise on television. In the fall of 1955 it ran six months of TV ads for a toy machine gun, and the gun sold out badly over Christmas. According to the book *Kids' Stuff: Toys and the Changing World of American Childhood*, Barbie first appeared in TV ads in 1959. Thanks to television, Mattel's sales rose from US$6 million in 1955 to US$49 million in 1961. Other toy companies soon followed. In 1971 Mattel spent US$20 million on TV advertising; Hasbro spent about US$6.5 million.

Today the talk is of television's decline, and these days you rarely hear of any fresh marketing for Barbie. That is why Mattel, despite raising its advertising spending by 40% in the fourth quarter of 2014, still posted dismal results.

Lego is the opposite case. The brick maker is enjoying a golden age of marketing. We have seen a Lego Oscars poster, a Lego Super Bowl ad, a Lego *Fifty Shades of Grey* trailer, a Lego *Jurassic Park* game, a game app tied to Lego *Legends of Chima*, and the hit *The Lego Movie*.

The chart below shows Lego's rapid growth in recent years. In 2011 Mattel's sales were still more than twice Lego's; in the first half of 2014 Lego overtook Mattel. Lego still finished the year behind Mattel, but its potential should not be underestimated.

![Chart: Lego vs. Mattel sales](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142424mnt4gZcLI3zqTSHO.jpg-w600)

Aging sales channels

Retailers, themselves battered by the internet, have also dragged down Barbie sales. Since 2010, store sales at Walmart, JCPenney, Target, Toys "R" Us and others have fallen steadily. These were once Barbie's main outlets; now they are struggling to cope with e-commerce.

In September 2014, the luxury e-commerce site Net-a-Porter sold a limited-edition Barbie online: a black-and-white "Barbie Lagerfeld" styled after Karl Lagerfeld. All 999 dolls, priced at US$200 each, sold out in moments. But a one-off stunt like this cannot transform a brand. And the buyers were probably drawn more by Lagerfeld's fame than by Barbie's.

### 5. Barbie, who once created toy pop culture, is being left behind by a new pop culture

Barbie first appeared as a rebel. She was no longer just a friendly playmate or a baby to be cared for, which had been the essence of doll play since the early 20th century. Barbie was not a child in children's clothes but a fashionable young woman with a shapely figure. In the 10 years after Barbie went on sale, only 60 of the more than 200 US doll companies survived. Barbie also cut into baby dolls: in 1959, when she launched, they made up 80% of all dolls; by 1975 they made up only 38%. Barbie once held a prime spot in every toy store.

Barbie was more than a toy. The tree-lined avenue in front of New York's Times Square was renamed Barbie Boulevard for a week, and the pop artist Andy Warhol painted her. The band Aqua wrote a single about her, "Barbie Girl," and Mattel ended up suing the band for infringement.

![Barbie in pop culture](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160607142425HYRc9EAsiCWpBfP6.jpg-w600)

Now, though, critics say Barbie's unrealistic body drives girls who imitate her toward anorexia, and an Oreo Barbie made with Nabisco was seen in African American communities as racist.

Meanwhile, as feminist thinking has deepened, society has come to see women's image and social standing differently. A tall, blonde, blue-eyed woman in a business suit or a princess gown is no longer the only future little girls imagine for themselves.

The clearest evidence: Bratz dolls, which sell a rebellious culture that is the exact opposite of Barbie's polished image, and Lego's line of female scientists were both snapped up as soon as they went on sale.

As Jim Silver, editor-in-chief of the toy magazine *Time to Play*, put it, the line between boys' and girls' toys is growing ever more blurred. Mothers such as Dawn Nadeau and Julie Kerwin have even crowdfunded IAmElemental female superhero dolls on Kickstarter to show their daughters strong female characters.

Society has changed and the market has changed, but the meaning of play has not. Mattel needs to set new trends in a new business climate, as it once did.
